entries.clue: Observer working with attractive person (8)

blocks.note: a machine that is working is on, the two letters printed on the switch
a looker is somebody worth looking at, the old compliment

annotation.surface: A watcher at work beside somebody good-looking.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Working' looks like employment and means switched on. 'Looker' is dated slang for a good-looking person, rarely heard now outside clues like this one.
annotation.definitionFit: An onlooker is one of the people standing round watching an event without joining in, which is what an observer does.

entries.clue: Dog, namely small Lhasa apso, taking leads (6)

indicatorNotes.taking leads: The lead is the front position in anything, so what is taken is the leading letter of each word named.

blocks.note: viz. is the printer's abbreviation of videlicet, used where we would say namely
s is the size on a clothing label
the opening letters of the two words; a Lhasa apso is a small long-haired Tibetan breed

annotation.surface: A small Lhasa apso being taken out on its lead.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leads' does two jobs at once: the dog's lead in the picture and the instruction underneath. The breed in the answer is the Hungarian pointer, a rust-coloured gundog.
annotation.definitionFit: The vizsla is a Hungarian gundog with a short russet coat, so dog is the plain class this breed belongs to.

entries.clue: Iron nut turned on new part of cannon, say (8)

indicatorNotes.turned: What has turned has come round out of the position it started in, so the letters beside it are not left in the order given.
indicatorNotes.say: Say offers the thing next to it as one instance of something wider, a cannon being only one of the guns mounted this way.

blocks.note: seven letters for the pile
n is the standard short form of new

annotation.surface: An iron nut being turned on a gun's new fitting.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is all ironmongery, which hides the ironmongery itself being the pile of letters. A trunnion is the stub each side of a barrel that lets the gun pivot in its carriage.
annotation.definitionFit: A trunnion is one of the pair of stubs projecting from a gun barrel and resting in the carriage, which is what lets the barrel tilt.

entries.clue: Year in Provence perhaps plugged by Times Supplement (6)

indicatorNotes.in Provence perhaps: Provence is in France, so the word in front of it is wanted in French, and perhaps allows the one region to stand for the whole country.
indicatorNotes.plugged by: A plug is pushed into a gap, so the letters named after it go inside the word before.

blocks.note: a year in French is an année, which loses its accent in a grid
x is the multiplication sign, the times of three x four

annotation.surface: Peter Mayle's A Year in Provence getting a plug in the Times supplement.
annotation.walkthrough: The italics flag Mayle's memoir, and 'Times Supplement' reads as the literary paper before splitting in two, one half wordplay and one half definition. Only the title's first word is wanted, and in French.
annotation.definitionFit: An annexe is matter added at the end of a document, the appendix or supplement that follows the main text.

entries.clue: Scottish author managed by family (6)

blocks.note: whoever managed a business ran it, and the past tense carries across
your kin are your family, the older word for them

annotation.surface: A Scottish author whose relatives are handling his affairs.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Managed by family' reads as one phrase about a firm and breaks into two pieces that simply sit side by side. Ian Rankin writes the Inspector Rebus novels, set in Edinburgh.
annotation.definitionFit: Ian Rankin is the Edinburgh crime novelist behind the Rebus books, so his surname is what Scottish author points to.

entries.clue: Where you might land fugitive, disheartened (6)

indicatorNotes.disheartened: A word disheartened has lost its heart, the single letter sitting at its centre.

blocks.note: a fugitive is a runaway, seven letters before the cut

annotation.surface: The place where an escaper might be caught coming down.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Land' pulls towards catching a fugitive, as in landing a fish, and is meant as an aircraft touching down. Only a word with an odd number of letters can be disheartened this cleanly.
annotation.definitionFit: A runway is the paved strip an aircraft comes down on, so it is precisely where you might land.

entries.clue: Engineer’s ancient letter kept by British Library (6)

indicatorNotes.kept by: What is kept by somebody is held inside their keeping, so the letters before go within the ones named after.

blocks.note: the British Library, the national library in London, is BL for short
a rune is a character of the old Germanic alphabet, carved rather than written

annotation.surface: An engineer's ancient letter looked after by the British Library.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Letter' is the alphabet kind rather than the posted kind, and the runic alphabet is where a clue usually finds an old one. Isambard Kingdom Brunel built the Great Western Railway and the Clifton suspension bridge.
annotation.definitionFit: Isambard Kingdom Brunel is the Victorian engineer of the Great Western Railway and the SS Great Britain, so his surname answers to engineer.

entries.clue: Note Yorkshire river ending in beautiful bay (6)

indicatorNotes.ending in: The ending of a word is the letter it stops on, and that single letter is all that is taken from the word named.

blocks.note: la is the sixth note of the sol-fa scale
the Ure runs down Wensleydale in North Yorkshire
the letter this word ends on

annotation.surface: A song about a Yorkshire river that finishes in a beautiful bay.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bay' is the tree rather than the inlet the surface paints: bay leaves come off a laurel. The Ure is one of the short Dales rivers setters keep coming back to.
annotation.definitionFit: The bay of the kitchen jar is a laurel, the same evergreen whose leaves were twisted into the classical wreath.

entries.clue: Composer’s poor aunt chokes after starter of soup (11)

indicatorNotes.poor: Something poor is in no fit state, and letters in that state are not left in the order they were given.
indicatorNotes.after: What comes after a thing follows it, so the jumbled letters are written behind the single letter.
indicatorNotes.starter of: The starter is what comes first at table and first in a word, so only the opening letter of the word behind is taken.

blocks.note: the opening letter of SOUP
ten letters for the pile

annotation.surface: A composer's hard-up aunt spluttering over the first course.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Starter of soup' is the menu word and a first-letter instruction in the same breath. Karlheinz Stockhausen was the German pioneer of electronic music, best known for Gesang der Jünglinge.
annotation.definitionFit: Karlheinz Stockhausen wrote the electronic and orchestral works that made him Germany's leading post-war composer.

entries.clue: Fancies girl among dozens? Not half (6)

indicatorNotes.among: What is among other things sits in the middle of them, so the name goes inside the letters left standing.
indicatorNotes.Not half: To have not half of a thing is to be left without half of it, and the word in front gives up three of its six letters.

blocks.note: the back half of DOZENS, three of its six letters
Joy is the girl's name, three letters dropped straight in

annotation.surface: Somebody takes a shine to one girl in a crowd of dozens.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dozens' is wanted for its spelling rather than its counting, and it keeps only its back half. 'Not half' is also the British idiom for an emphatic yes, which is the tone the surface borrows.
annotation.definitionFit: To fancy a thing is to like it and to enjoy it is to take pleasure in it, the same liking and both in the third person.

entries.clue: Plastered punk date abandoned (6,2)

indicatorNotes.abandoned: Abandoned behaviour is behaviour with the restraints off, and letters let loose that way do not stay in the order given.

blocks.note: eight letters for the pile

annotation.surface: A drunken punk whose date has walked out on him.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Plastered' is the drunk sense, not the decorator's. 'Abandoned' looks like the date leaving and means unrestrained, which is the sense that lets it shuffle letters.
annotation.definitionFit: To be tanked up is to be full of drink, which is exactly what plastered says of somebody.

entries.clue: Communicate unfinished story by king (4)

indicatorNotes.unfinished: What is unfinished stops short of its end, so the word beside it never reaches its final letter.

blocks.note: a story is a TALE, and the deletion takes its last letter off
k is the king of chess notation and of the card pack

annotation.surface: A story left half-told by a king.
annotation.walkthrough: 'By' joins the two pieces in the order the clue gives them and contributes nothing itself. K is one of the letters a solver meets most often, since king, kilo and thousand all reduce to it.
annotation.definitionFit: To talk is to communicate in speech, the same verb in the same plain form.

entries.clue: Greek scientist heads crime broadcast (10)

indicatorNotes.broadcast: To broadcast seed is to scatter it wide over a field, and scattered letters do not keep the order given.

blocks.note: ten letters for the pile

annotation.surface: A Greek scientist fronting a television bulletin about crime.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Heads' reads as leading a programme and is simply part of the pile; no word is giving up its first letter. Archimedes worked at Syracuse in Sicily and was killed there in 212 BC.
annotation.definitionFit: Archimedes of Syracuse was the Greek mathematician of the lever, the screw and the bath, so Greek scientist names him by his trade.

entries.clue: Eccentric name that started up old saloon? (11)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a relative clause rather than a noun, describing the answer by what it used to do instead of naming it.

blocks.note: a crank is an eccentric, the oddball sense of the noun
a handle is slang for a name, the word CB radio users gave their own

annotation.surface: An oddball whose name once got an old car going.
annotation.walkthrough: A saloon is the British word for what Americans call a sedan, and before starter motors a driver swung a handle at the front of the car to turn the engine over. In machinery a crank is an eccentric too.
annotation.definitionFit: A crank handle is the lever a driver turned by hand to start an engine, the fitting cars carried before electric starters arrived.

entries.clue: Bulbous growths seen in blurred iris scan (8)

indicatorNotes.blurred: A blurred picture has lost its sharp arrangement, and letters described that way are not in the order given.

blocks.note: eight letters for the pile

annotation.surface: A biometric eye scan that has come out out of focus.
annotation.walkthrough: The iris here is the eye at the airport gate, while the other iris, the garden one, stands one flowerbed away from the answer. Narcissi are the daffodil tribe.
annotation.definitionFit: Narcissi come up each spring from bulbs planted in the autumn, so bulbous growths describes how these plants grow.

entries.clue: Rake knotted hair with tool (8)

indicatorNotes.knotted: Hair that is knotted has tangled out of its proper order, and tangled letters do not stay as they were given.

blocks.note: four letters for the pile
four more letters for the pile

annotation.surface: Dragging a garden tool through matted hair.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rake' opens as the implement lying beside the hair and is the definition, in its old sense of a man about town. Lothario is the seducer in Nicholas Rowe's 1703 play The Fair Penitent.
annotation.definitionFit: A rake is a man who lives loosely and chases women, which is what the name Lothario has come to stand for.

entries.clue: Eg translating from German, and in German (6)

blocks.note: Ger. is the standard short form of German
und is the German word for and

annotation.surface: Somebody translating out of German runs into the word for 'and'.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves lean on the same language, the country's short form and its little word for 'and'. A gerund is the -ing form of a verb doing a noun's job, which is why 'translating' is only an example of one.
annotation.definitionFit: A gerund is a verb's -ing form used as a noun, so 'translating' in 'translating is slow work' is one instance of the class.

entries.clue: Fish particular spot around island (6)

indicatorNotes.around: What goes around a thing encircles it, so the letters before close over the single letter named after.

blocks.note: a particular spot is a place, five letters that open to take the insertion
i is the map-maker's short form of island

annotation.surface: Fishing one particular spot in the water round an island.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Particular spot' hands over a whole five-letter word rather than a single letter of it, which is the harder reading to see. The plaice is the orange-spotted flatfish sold battered in British chip shops.
annotation.definitionFit: The plaice is a North Sea flatfish, the brown one freckled with orange spots that fills most British fish suppers.

entries.clue: Potter surnamed so unusually (4,6)

indicatorNotes.unusually: What is done unusually is not done the usual way, so the letters beside it do not keep their usual order.

blocks.note: ten letters for the pile

annotation.surface: A Potter whose surname is spelt in some unusual way.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Potter' wants to be a person, Harry or Beatrix, and is the British verb for drifting about with nothing much to do. The capital letter is only there because the clue starts on it.
annotation.definitionFit: To potter is the British verb for busying yourself with nothing in particular, which is what messing around describes.

entries.clue: I’m not quite sure boy keeps address (6)

indicatorNotes.keeps: To keep a thing is to hold on to it, so the boy closes around the letters named before him.

blocks.note: a boy is a son, three letters that open up to take the rest
erm is the noise people make while they hunt for the next word

annotation.surface: Somebody hesitating over whether the boy has kept an address.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Address' is the talk given from a pulpit, not the one written on an envelope. A whole phrase of hesitation stands in for three letters, which is more hiding than a short word would manage.
annotation.definitionFit: A sermon is the address a preacher delivers from the pulpit, so the noun for a formal talk covers it.

entries.clue: Read up about quiet reindeer (6)

indicatorNotes.up: In a down clue what runs up is read from the foot of the column, so the word before it is spelt backwards.
indicatorNotes.about: What goes about a thing wraps round it, so the letters named after sit inside the ones already turned.

blocks.note: READ written the other way up the column
sh is the hiss that asks for quiet

annotation.surface: Somebody reading up about a quiet reindeer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Read up about' is one phrase in the surface and three separate instructions underneath. Dasher is the first of the eight reindeer named in the 1823 poem 'A Visit from St Nicholas'.
annotation.definitionFit: Dasher heads the team of reindeer in the Christmas poem, the first name called out as the sleigh leaves.

entries.clue: Unintroduced foul narrative (4)

indicatorNotes.Unintroduced: An introduction is what comes at the front, so a word left unintroduced loses its first letter.

blocks.note: the air in a shut room goes foul, which is to say stale

annotation.surface: A foul story that nobody bothered to introduce.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Foul' points at something disgusting and is wanted in the milder sense of air gone stale. 'Unintroduced' is a rarer way of asking for a beheading than the usual 'headless'.
annotation.definitionFit: A tale is a story as it is told, which is what a narrative is: an account of events set out in order.

entries.clue: Statistical group trial scrapped in Quebec (8)

indicatorNotes.scrapped: Scrapped machinery is broken up for its parts, and letters broken up that way do not keep their order.
indicatorNotes.in: In puts whatever comes before it inside whatever comes after, so the broken letters land within the province.

blocks.note: the Canadian province Quebec is Que. for short
the five letters of TRIAL rearranged

annotation.surface: A drug trial dropped by a research group out in Quebec.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Quebec' is the province here rather than the radio alphabet's Q, which is the single letter most clues want from that word. Three of its letters are needed, wrapped round the rest.
annotation.definitionFit: A quartile is one of the four equal groups a ranked set of figures divides into, which is a statistician's way of grouping data.

entries.clue: Still, it may affect reception (6)

blocks.note: the motionless sense: what does not move is still
the radio sense: the crackle and hiss that spoil a signal

annotation.surface: Nothing is moving, and the picture on the set is breaking up.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma makes 'Still' read as a concession opening the sentence, when it is a definition standing on its own. Both senses trace back to electric charge that sits without flowing and crackles when it lets go.
annotation.definitionFit: Still means motionless, and the interference that spoils a radio or television signal carries the same name, charge that sits rather than flows.

entries.clue: Sluggish doctor that hurts somebody’s skin (6)

indicatorNotes.skin: Skin is what lies on the outside of a body, so only the outermost letters of the word before it are taken.

blocks.note: dr is the everyday short form of doctor
ow is the two-letter yelp you let out when something hurts
the first and last letters of SOMEBODY

annotation.surface: A doctor pressing somebody's sore skin.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a consulting room and every word of it is doing a different job underneath. 'Skin' for the outer letters belongs with shell, jacket and coat, which all ask for the same thing.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody drowsy is half asleep and slow with it, which is the sluggishness the adjective describes.

entries.clue: Damage extremely delicate tool (6)

indicatorNotes.extremely: Extremely points at the extremes of the word beside it, the letters standing at each end.

blocks.note: the first and last letters of DELICATE
a file is the toolbox's rasp for smoothing metal

annotation.surface: Damage done to an extremely delicate tool.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' looks like an intensifier for the tool and is an instruction to strip a word to its ends. The answer is also the noun for a narrow pass between hills, from a different root.
annotation.definitionFit: To defile something is to spoil or dirty it, which is damage done to the state a thing is in.
